`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The reverse-prompt move shifts the bottleneck. Planning docs usually leave **the user as the rate-limiter** (you need to call X, look up Y, decide Z). The valuable inversion is asking: "what work can be pre-staged so when the user *does* have 10 minutes, the next concrete step is 30 seconds, not a fishing expedition?"
- Most autonomous artifacts fall in three buckets: **pre-staging** (work that compresses your future 10-min windows), **calculators** (parameterize the unknowns so plugging in real numbers later is trivial), and **tracking infrastructure** (issues, templates, files that make state observable).
- The right calibration is to default-build the **pre-staging** tier (it has direct expected value) and only build calculators/trackers if you'll actually look at them — otherwise it's planning-of-planning.

## How approval works

Per session memory (`feedback_never_offer_self_label_plan_approved`), I won't auto-execute. Greenlight options:

- **"approve all"** — execute all 4 with default answers to open questions
- **"approve #N"** — execute one (specify by number)
- **"approve #N, Q2=X, Q3=Y"** — execute with explicit answers to specific open questions
- **"hold #N"** — keep the plan filed but don't execute yet
- **"reject #N because Z"** — close the issue with reasoning so the rejection is logged

## My recommendation on sequencing

If you want to greenlight all four eventually, do them in this order:

1. **#79 first** (NW glidepath) — fastest payoff; the moment #77 closes you get an updated #73 in one command
2. **#80 next** (SNT sizing) — feeds concrete numbers into #75 and #76 before those consults happen
3. **#81 third** (risk matrix) — most useful when it precedes the #75 consult by ~1 week so it can shape the question list
4. **#82 last** (Gate-1 prep) — lowest urgency (4 years out); no penalty for filing later

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- I deliberately put **"open questions"** at the bottom of each plan rather than at the top. They're the lowest-effort approval-friction lever — you can scan the plan, decide whether the scope is right, and *then* answer questions only on the ones you're approving. Putting questions at the top would force a full review just to figure out whether to engage.
- The four plans **share no dependencies** with each other, which is why parallel approval works. The only ordering constraint is that #79 becomes *more* valuable after #77 closes (real Fidelity baseline) — but #79 itself can be built before then with placeholder inputs.
- Each plan's **"AWAITING USER REVIEW"** marker is in the issue body, not a label, because the available labels in this repo don't include a `status:plan-review` analog. The text marker is what makes the gate observable; a future repo-level enhancement would be to add status labels per the workspace-hub planning-mode convention.
